title: Gundy v. United States (2019)
summary: A fractured Court upheld SORNA’s grant to the Attorney General of authority to specify the statute’s application to pre-Act offenders: Kagan’s four-Justice plurality read the Act to require registration of pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving only transitional details, while Alito concurred in the judgment under existing doctrine and Gorsuch, Roberts and Thomas would have held the delegation unconstitutional.

sections.Parties: Herman Avery Gundy was the criminal defendant in the Southern District of New York, the appellant in the Second Circuit and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The United States prosecuted him for failing to register under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) and defended his conviction. Gundy argued that Congress unconstitutionally delegated legislative power when it authorized the Attorney General to specify SORNA’s applicability to people convicted before the Act.
sections.Material Facts: Section 20913(a) requires an offender to register and keep the registration current where he lives, works or studies; § 20913(b) sets the initial deadline, before release from prison or within three business days of a nonprison sentence. Section 20913(d), the challenged provision, authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of the requirements to offenders convicted before enactment. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2250(a) a registrant who travels interstate and knowingly fails to register faces up to ten years in prison. The Attorney General issued an interim rule in February 2007 and a final rule in December 2010 applying SORNA to all pre-Act offenders. Gundy had pleaded guilty in Maryland in 2005 to a sexual offense involving a minor. While serving a later federal sentence he traveled by bus from Pennsylvania to a Bronx reentry center on July 17, 2012 and never registered in Maryland or New York.
sections.Procedural History: The district court first dismissed the indictment, but the Second Circuit reinstated it, holding that Gundy was required to register no later than August 1, 2008, 804 F.3d 140 (2015). After a bench trial on stipulated facts the district court found the elements proved and on June 16, 2016 sentenced him to time served and five years of supervised release. The Second Circuit affirmed on June 22, 2017, 695 F. App’x 639, rejecting the nondelegation argument as foreclosed by circuit precedent. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on the nondelegation question only, heard argument on October 2, 2018, and affirmed on June 20, 2019. Justice Kagan announced the judgment for a plurality (Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor); Justice Alito concurred in the judgment; Justice Gorsuch dissented with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas; Justice Kavanaugh did not participate.
sections.Issue: Does Congress violate Article I’s vesting of legislative power when it authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of SORNA’s registration requirements to offenders convicted before the statute’s enactment? Read with the rest of SORNA, does § 20913(d) require registration of all pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving transitional decisions, or does it let the Attorney General decide whether, when and to what extent they are covered at all?
sections.Holding: The Court affirmed the conviction 5–3. The plurality held that the scope of a delegation must be fixed by statutory interpretation before its constitutionality is assessed, construed SORNA to require the Attorney General to apply the registration requirements to pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, and held that this limited assignment easily satisfied the intelligible-principle test; the words “as soon as feasible” are the plurality’s construction, not statutory text. Alito supplied the fifth vote because he could not say the statute lacked a discernible standard under existing doctrine, but he joined neither Kagan’s reading nor her reasoning. Neither the plurality’s analysis nor the dissent’s proposed test is a five-Justice holding.
sections.Reasoning: Kagan began with the relationship between interpretation and nondelegation: a court cannot judge the adequacy of Congress’s instructions until it knows what authority the statute confers. Reynolds v. United States had held that SORNA did not apply to pre-Act offenders until the Attorney General acted, but the plurality read Reynolds as recognizing only a practical reason for delay: the need to bring a large existing population into the system. The declaration of purpose announced a comprehensive national system, § 20913(d)’s pairing with rulemaking authority for offenders unable to comply with subsection (b) marked it as a transition provision. So read, the Attorney General could weigh administrative difficulties but could not decline indefinitely to register pre-Act offenders; the limit came from the statute, not from the official’s restraint. Gorsuch, dissenting, tied nondelegation to bicameralism, presentment and accountability, and would allow Congress only to let others fill in details after fixing policy, make a rule contingent on executive fact-finding, or assign nonlegislative duties; SORNA fit none, because deciding which pre-Act offenders face criminally enforceable duties is the coverage choice itself.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: The plurality upheld a construed feasibility delegation, and Alito concurred under existing permissive precedent.
topics.lrs-s-details: Gorsuch’s dissent distinguished legislative policy from administrative details and challenged whether SORNA made the necessary policy choice.
topics.lrs-s-accountability: The opinions disagree over whether flexible administration or retained legislative responsibility better preserves constitutional accountability.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Alito, concurring in the judgment, agreed that Congress may not transfer legislative power but observed that since 1935 the Court had upheld very broad delegations under capacious standards; he would support reconsidering the doctrine if a majority were willing, but would not single out this statute under a newly demanding approach. Justice Gorsuch, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, would have held the delegation unconstitutional. FCC v. Consumers’ Research (2025) later applied the intelligible-principle framework and upheld the universal-service delegation, Kagan writing for six Justices including Roberts, Kavanaugh and Barrett.
